mainTopic: כבוד הבריות vs. Torah law: the consolers' row, כלאים in public, and the sources that seem to let honor override prohibitions
overview: The גמרא first explains the משנה's rule about consolers standing in a row (שורה), who are exempt from קריאת שמע. A ברייתא gives two tests. The תנא קמא asks whether the row can see the mourners, and רבי יהודה asks whether the people came for the mourner's sake. The גמרא then asks a wider question: does כבוד הבריות push aside Torah law? רב rules that someone who finds כלאים on his clothes must take them off even in the market, because 'there is no wisdom against ה׳'. Wherever there is חילול השם, we do not give honor even to a רב. The גמרא tests this rule against three sources. Walking a טמא path for a mourner is explained as a בית הפרס, which is only rabbinic. כהנים jumping over coffins to greet kings broke only a rabbinic decree. The ברייתא saying dignity overrides a 'Torah prohibition' really means rabbinic laws, which lean on לא תסור. The lost-object case is a real Torah exception, but it is about money, so it cannot teach rules about איסור. Finally, the גמרא begins a ברייתא about a נזיר and a מת מצוה, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which row of consolers is exempt from קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the row of consolers and brings a ברייתא: a row that can see the mourners is exempt, and a row that cannot see them is obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the משנה's words 'those standing in the row': the Rabbis taught that a row that sees inside, where the mourners are, is exempt from קריאת שמע. A row that does not see inside is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up a line from the משנה about consolers standing in rows. It brings a ברייתא that explains which row counts as exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said only the inner row is exempt and did not say exactly what makes a row 'inner'. The ברייתא gives the test: can the row actually see the mourners? If they can see them, they are really part of the comforting and are exempt. If not, they must say שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: A row of people lined up to comfort the mourners after the burial
Sees inside, meaning the row can see the mourners

phrases.english: 'Those standing in the row,' etc.
The Rabbis taught:
A row that sees inside is exempt,
and one that does not see inside is obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה's line about the row of consolers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A row of consolers that can see the mourners is exempt from קריאת שמע; a row that cannot see them is obligated.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: it depends on why they came
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that people who came for the mourner's sake are exempt, and those who came for their own reasons are obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: those who came because of the mourner are exempt. Those who came for their own sake are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a different test for the row of consolers. He looks at why each person came, not at where he is standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא's test is physical: can you see the mourners? רבי יהודה's test is about intention: did you come to comfort the mourner, or just to watch? Only someone busy with the מצוה of comforting is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of the mourner, meaning to comfort him
For their own sake, such as curiosity or to be seen

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Those who come because of the mourner are exempt,
those who come for their own sake are obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second opinion in the same ברייתא, using intention as the test instead of seeing the mourners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Exemption depends on whether the person came to comfort the mourner or came for himself.
steps.whatToRemember: Two tests for the exempt row: the תנא קמא asks whether they can see the mourners, and רבי יהודה asks whether they came for the mourner's sake.

steps.title: Finding כלאים on your clothes in public
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that someone who finds כלאים in his garment must take it off right away, even in the marketplace.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: someone who finds כלאים in his garment takes it off even in the market.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to a wider topic: does a person's honor push aside a Torah prohibition? רב says no. You must take off a garment of כלאים immediately, even in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking off clothing in the market is embarrassing, so we might think he could wait until he gets home. רב says he may not wait. Avoiding a Torah איסור comes before his own dignity.

keyTerms.meaning: A forbidden mix, here wool and linen in one garment (שעטנז)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
One who finds כלאים in his garment
takes them off even in the marketplace.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the specific case of consolers to the general question of human dignity against Torah law.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who discovers כלאים on himself must remove it at once, even in public.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rule that the rest of the סוגיא tests: human dignity does not override a Torah prohibition.

steps.title: The source: no wisdom against ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for רב's reason and brings the פסוק 'there is no wisdom, understanding, or counsel against ה׳'. From it comes the rule that where there is חילול השם, we do not give honor even to a רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Because the פסוק says 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against ה׳.' So anywhere there is חילול השם, we do not give honor even to a teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב rules this way, and it answers with a פסוק from משלי. This produces a big general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק teaches that no human consideration can stand against ה׳'s will. If that is true even of a רב's honor, then it is certainly true of a person's own embarrassment. Breaking a Torah law is a חילול השם, and honor does not override it.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not give honor to the teacher

phrases.english: What is the reason?
'There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against ה׳.'
Any place where there is a desecration of ה׳'s name,
we do not give honor to the teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural basis for רב's ruling about כלאים.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that one removes כלאים even in public
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי 21:30, 'There is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel against ה׳'
steps.whatToRemember: The rule: wherever there is חילול השם, honor, even a רב's honor, does not count.

steps.title: Challenge: walking on an impure path for a mourner's honor
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if the mourner takes the impure path home from the burial, everyone goes with him on the impure path to honor him. That seems to put human honor above Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: they buried the dead and were returning, and there were two paths ahead, one pure and one impure. If the mourner went on the pure path, they went with him on the pure path. If he went on the impure path, they went with him on the impure path, out of respect for him. Why? Let us say 'There is no wisdom and no understanding against ה׳'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rule from the last step. It quotes a ברייתא where people seem to become טמא just to honor a mourner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If honor never overrides a prohibition, how can people walk on a path of טומאה, which may include כהנים who are forbidden to become טמא, only for a mourner's honor? This looks like exactly what the פסוק forbids.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection, from a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: 'He' in this ברייתא is the mourner. The others follow whichever path he chooses.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
They buried the dead and returned,
and before them were two paths,
one pure and one impure.
If he goes on the pure one, they go with him on the pure one;
if he goes on the impure one, they go with him on the impure one
because of his honor.
Why?

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא ״אֵין חׇכְמָה וְאֵין תְּבוּנָה לְנֶגֶד ה׳״!
phrases.english: Let us say 'There is no wisdom and no understanding against ה׳'!
phrases.notes: The same פסוק from step 4 is being turned back against this ברייתא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the principle from step 4 with a ברייתא that seems to contradict it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that wherever there is חילול השם, human honor does not count
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lets people take on טומאה for a mourner's honor, which seems to put human honor above a Torah prohibition.

steps.title: רבי אבא: the path is only impure מדרבנן
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא explains that the impure path in the ברייתא is a בית הפרס, which is only impure by rabbinic law, so honor can override it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא explained the ברייתא as talking about a בית הפרס, which is impure only by rabbinic law.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא answers the challenge by narrowing what the 'impure path' is. It is a field that is only rabbinically impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בית הפרס is a field where a grave was plowed over. חז״ל treat the whole field as טמא in case bones were scattered, but by Torah law it is not impure. The פסוק's rule applies to Torah prohibitions. For a rabbinic rule, a mourner's honor can push it aside.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, meaning he gave the ברייתא a specific reading
A field where a grave was plowed up; it is impure out of doubt about scattered bones
By rabbinic law, not Torah law

steps.whatToRemember: Human honor does not override a Torah prohibition, but it can override a rabbinic one such as בית הפרס.
steps.whyThisMatters: This draws the line for the whole סוגיא: כבוד הבריות pushes aside rabbinic laws, not Torah laws.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba explained it
as a בית הפרס, which is rabbinic.
phrases.notes: A field where a grave was plowed over. The Rabbis call it impure, but the Torah does not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 5 by limiting the ברייתא to rabbinic impurity.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ברייתא is about a path that is only impure מדרבנן
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'impure path' seemed to be impure by Torah law, so honor would be overriding a Torah prohibition.
steps.terutzMaskana: The path is a בית הפרס, impure only מדרבנן, and a mourner's honor can override a rabbinic rule. The principle 'no wisdom against ה׳' still holds for Torah prohibitions.

steps.title: Proof that בית הפרס is only a rabbinic impurity
steps.stepSummary: Two rulings show that the Rabbis were lenient about בית הפרס. You may blow away the dust to check for bones, and a trampled בית הפרס is pure. That leniency only makes sense for a rabbinic impurity.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: a person may blow on the ground of a בית הפרס as he walks through it. And רב יהודה בר אשי said in the name of רב: a בית הפרס that has been trampled down is pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבי אבא's answer from step 6. It brings two rulings showing that בית הפרס impurity is handled loosely, which proves it is rabbinic and not from the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a real Torah impurity, you could not rely on blowing away dust to check for bones, and you could not call the ground pure just because people walked over it. Since the Rabbis allow both, בית הפרס must be their own extra stringency. That is why honoring a mourner can override it.

keyTerms.meaning: Blows (on the dust, to uncover any bones)
A field where a grave was plowed over, so bone pieces may be scattered in it; impure only by rabbinic law
Trampled, trodden down into a path

steps.whyThisMatters: This confirms the line between rabbinic law, which honor can override, and Torah law, which it cannot. The rest of the סוגיא depends on that line.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
A person may blow his way through a beit haperas and walk on.
phrases.notes: He blows the dust away in front of him so he can see any bones and step around them.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בַּר אָשֵׁי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda bar Ashi said in the name of Rav:
A beit haperas that has been trampled is pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אבא's claim that בית הפרס is only rabbinic
steps.raayaObject: רבי אבא's claim that בית הפרס impurity is only rabbinic
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's ruling about blowing on the dust, and רב's ruling that a trampled בית הפרס is pure

steps.title: כהנים jumping over coffins to greet kings
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק says that he and other כהנים jumped over coffins to greet kings, even non-Jewish kings. The גמרא asks why honor should beat a Torah prohibition when the פסוק says there is no counsel against ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אלעזר בר צדוק said, 'We would jump over coffins of the dead to go greet the kings of Israel.' And this was not said only for kings of Israel. It applies even to kings of the nations, so that if a person merits, he will see the difference between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations. Why is that allowed? Let us say: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against ה׳!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to show human honor overriding Torah law. It challenges that source with the same פסוק used in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן may not become impure from a dead body, and that is a Torah prohibition. Here כהנים seem to break it just to honor a king. That clashes with the rule from step 4 that honor does not override a Torah law when there is חילול השם.

keyTerms.meaning: We would jump or leap over

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר צָדוֹק:
phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said:

phrases.aramaic: מְדַלְּגִין הָיִינוּ עַל גַּבֵּי אֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁל מֵתִים,
phrases.english: We would jump over coffins of the dead
phrases.notes: He was a כהן, and a כהן isn't allowed to become impure from a dead body.

phrases.english: to go greet the kings of Israel.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּלְבַד אָמְרוּ
phrases.english: And they did not say this only for going to greet kings of Israel,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: but even for going to greet kings of the nations of the world,
so that if he merits,

phrases.aramaic: יַבְחִין בֵּין מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: he will tell the difference between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations of the world.
Why?
Let us say: "There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against ה׳!"
phrases.notes: משלי 21:30, the same פסוק from step 4.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּר צָדוֹק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new source that challenges the principle from step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that honor does not override a Torah prohibition (step 4)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כהנים broke the Torah ban on becoming impure from the dead just to honor kings, so honor seems to beat Torah law.

steps.title: רבא's rule: a handbreadth of space blocks impurity
steps.stepSummary: The answer starts with רבא's rule. By Torah law, a covering with a טפח of empty space blocks impurity from spreading upward. Without that space, it does not block it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רבא's teaching. רבא said: by Torah law, any tent (covering) that has a handbreadth of empty space blocks the impurity. One without a handbreadth of space does not block the impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by bringing רבא's rule about when a covering blocks impurity. This sets up the next step, which applies the rule to coffins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a covering over a dead body has at least a טפח of open space, the impurity stays inside and does not reach someone above it. This means a person jumping over such a coffin may not be breaking any Torah law at all.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law (as opposed to rabbinic law)
A tent, or any covering over a source of impurity
An empty space of one handbreadth

phrases.english: It is like Rava's teaching.
For Rava said: By Torah law, a tent,
any one that has an empty space of a handbreadth
phrases.notes: He means open space between the body and the covering above it.

phrases.english: blocks the impurity.
And one that does not have an empty space of a handbreadth
does not block the impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the challenge in step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the case: jumping over the coffins was not a Torah violation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Jumping over coffins breaks the Torah ban on a כהן becoming impure
steps.terutzMaskana: By Torah law, a coffin with a handbreadth of space blocks the impurity

steps.title: The ban is rabbinic, and kings' honor sets it aside
steps.stepSummary: Most coffins have a טפח of space, so by Torah law they block impurity. The Rabbis banned all coffins because of the few without space. For the honor of kings, they did not apply their decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Most coffins have a handbreadth of empty space. The Rabbis made a decree about coffins that have the space because of the coffins that do not. But for the honor of kings, the Rabbis did not make the decree apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by applying רבא's rule to coffins. Jumping over them is only forbidden by a rabbinic decree, and that decree was lifted to honor kings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because most coffins block impurity by Torah law, the only problem is the Rabbis' extra decree. A rabbinic decree can give way to honor, so רבי אלעזר בר צדוק's practice does not show honor overriding Torah law. The rule from step 4 still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: They (the Rabbis) made a protective decree

steps.whatToRemember: Honor can push aside a rabbinic rule, like בית הפרס or the decree about coffins. It does not push aside a real Torah prohibition. Both sources that seemed to show otherwise turned out to be rabbinic cases.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the כהנים ignored a Torah law. By Torah law the coffin itself blocked the impurity, so only the Rabbis' extra decree was set aside.

phrases.aramaic: וְרוֹב אֲרוֹנוֹת יֵשׁ בָּהֶן חָלָל טֶפַח.
phrases.english: And most coffins have an empty space of a handbreadth.
And the Rabbis made a decree about those that have it
because of those that do not have it.
But because of the honor of kings,
the Rabbis did not make the decree apply to them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרוֹב אֲרוֹנוֹת יֵשׁ בָּהֶן חָלָל טֶפַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's rule from step 9 to finish the answer
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the prohibition being overridden is only rabbinic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כהנים broke a Torah law to honor kings
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a rabbinic decree was involved, and the Rabbis did not apply it when honoring kings

steps.title: A ברייתא says dignity overrides a Torah prohibition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying that כבוד הבריות pushes aside a לא תעשה in the Torah. It asks how that can be, since the פסוק says there is no counsel against ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Human dignity is so great that it pushes aside a Torah prohibition. But why? We should say here too: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding and no counsel against ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that seems to let human dignity beat a Torah prohibition. Then it asks how that fits with the rule that nothing can stand against ה׳'s command.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps limited dignity to pushing aside rabbinic rules, like בית הפרס and the rabbinic decree about coffins. This ברייתא seems to say openly that dignity beats a Torah לא תעשה. So it clashes with the פסוק אין חכמה ואין עצה לנגד ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: Human dignity, the honor owed to every person
A negative commandment, something the Torah forbids

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Great is human dignity,
for it pushes aside a prohibition in the Torah.
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in square brackets. Either way, the meaning is the same.

phrases.english: But why? Let us say:
"There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against ה׳"!
phrases.notes: משלי 21:30. This is the same פסוק רב used in step 4.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source that challenges the same principle from step 4, after the coffin challenge (steps 8–10) was settled.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle that human dignity cannot override a Torah prohibition (אין עצה לנגד ה׳).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא openly says dignity pushes aside a Torah לא תעשה, which seems to go against the פסוק.

steps.title: רב בר שבא says the ברייתא means the prohibition of לא תסור
steps.stepSummary: רב בר שבא explains that the 'Torah prohibition' in the ברייתא is the לאו of לא תסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב בר שבא explained it in front of רב כהנא: the ברייתא is talking about the prohibition of 'Do not stray.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב בר שבא answers the question. He says the ברייתא is talking about one specific prohibition, לא תסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He narrows the ברייתא's 'Torah prohibition' down to לא תסור, the command not to stray from what the חכמים teach. At this point it isn't clear why that one would be different, so the next step challenges it.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, he interpreted it
"Do not stray." The command to obey the rulings of the חכמים

phrases.english: רב בר שבא explained it
in front of רב כהנא:
as the prohibition of "Do not stray."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing which prohibition the ברייתא means
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lets dignity override any Torah prohibition.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only means the prohibition of לא תסור.

steps.title: The students laugh: לא תסור is also a Torah law
steps.stepSummary: The listeners laugh at רב בר שבא, because לא תסור is itself a Torah prohibition, so the problem hasn't gone away.
steps.simpleTranslation: They laughed at him. Isn't the prohibition of 'Do not stray' a Torah law?!
steps.whatsHappening: The people listening make fun of the answer. They point out that לא תסור is also a Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dignity overrides לא תסור, it is still overriding a Torah prohibition. So the answer seems to leave the original question exactly where it was.

phrases.english: They laughed at him:
isn't the prohibition of "Do not stray" a Torah law?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer from step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב בר שבא's claim that the ברייתא means לא תסור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: לא תסור is a Torah prohibition too, so the question of אין עצה לנגד ה׳ is still there.

steps.title: רב כהנא explains: the ברייתא really means rabbinic rules
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא defends רב בר שבא. All rabbinic laws lean on לא תסור, so the ברייתא is really talking about rabbinic rules, and the חכמים allowed dignity to override them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: A great man said something, don't laugh at him. The חכמים leaned all rabbinic rules on the prohibition of 'Do not stray,' and because of a person's dignity, the חכמים permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא tells the students not to laugh and explains what רב בר שבא meant. 'לא תסור' is a way of saying 'rabbinic laws.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every rabbinic rule draws its force from the Torah command of לא תסור, so breaking one can be called breaking a Torah prohibition. But the actual rule being set aside is rabbinic. The חכמים who made it chose to let dignity override it, so nothing goes against ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: A great man, a great scholar
They leaned them, they based them

steps.whatToRemember: כבוד הבריות can push aside rabbinic rules, which lean on לא תסור, but it cannot push aside a regular Torah prohibition.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא says 'a prohibition in the Torah,' but in the end it does not mean that dignity overrides real Torah laws. It only means rabbinic rules, which get their force from the Torah's command of לא תסור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a key rule for הלכה: concern for human dignity can set aside rabbinic laws, but not a Torah law.

phrases.english: רב כהנא said:
A great man said something,
don't laugh at him.
All rabbinic rules
they based on the prohibition of "Do not stray,"
and because of a person's dignity, the חכמים permitted it.
phrases.notes: "It" means setting aside their own rabbinic rule when it clashes with a person's dignity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the students' challenge from step 13 and explains the answer from step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the term: לא תסור stands for all rabbinic laws
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Overriding לא תסור means overriding a real Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rules being set aside are rabbinic. Their authors allowed dignity to override them, so nothing stands against ה׳.

steps.title: A new source: sometimes you may ignore a lost object
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא on the פסוק about returning lost objects: sometimes you may ignore them, and sometimes you may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And ignore them.' This teaches that sometimes you may ignore lost objects, and sometimes you may not ignore them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It brings a new source about returning lost objects that will be tested against the rule about dignity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to forbid ignoring a lost animal, but the ברייתא reads the word והתעלמת as teaching that sometimes ignoring it is allowed. Returning a lost object is a Torah מצוה. So if dignity is a reason to ignore it, this would look like dignity overriding a Torah law.

keyTerms.meaning: "And you will ignore." From the פסוק about lost objects

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And ignore them":
phrases.notes: דברים 22:1, the פסוק about seeing your brother's lost ox or sheep.

phrases.english: sometimes you ignore them,
and sometimes you do not ignore them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 14 settles the first ברייתא, the גמרא brings another source to test the same principle.
steps.raayaObject: Whether dignity can override a Torah מצוה, here the מצוה of returning a lost object.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on דברים 22:1: sometimes you may ignore a lost object.

steps.title: When you may ignore a lost object
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists three cases where a person may ignore a lost object: a כהן when the object is in a cemetery, a זקן when it is beneath his dignity, and someone whose own work matters more.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does this work? If he was a כהן and the object was in a cemetery, or he was an elder and handling it was beneath his dignity, or his own work was worth more than his friend's, then for these cases the Torah says 'and you shall disregard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step now explains when you are allowed to ignore a lost object. The middle case, the זקן, is about dignity, and that is the case that matters for our סוגיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said that 'sometimes you may ignore it and sometimes you may not.' Now we get the details. The זקן case shows a person's dignity letting him skip a Torah מצוה, and that is exactly the kind of case the גמרא is looking for.

keyTerms.meaning: A priest, who may not become impure from the dead
An elder, an honored older person

phrases.english: How so?
If he was a priest,
and it was in the cemetery,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the lost object. A כהן may not enter a cemetery to get it.

phrases.english: or he was an elder
and it is not fitting for his dignity,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה מְלַאכְתּוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִשֶּׁל חֲבֵרוֹ,
phrases.english: or his own work was greater than that of his friend,
for this it is said: "and you shall disregard."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא started in Step 15 by listing its cases.
steps.raayaObject: That dignity can let a person skip the Torah מצוה of returning a lost object.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'וְהִתְעַלַּמְתָּ', in the case of the זקן.

steps.title: Why doesn't 'no counsel against ה׳' apply here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the זקן may ignore the lost object. We should apply the rule that 'there is no wisdom or counsel against ה׳.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let us say: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against ה׳!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא. If dignity never beats a Torah law, how can the זקן ignore a lost object?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is רב's פסוק from Step 4, which the גמרא has already used to challenge earlier sources. Here the גמרא turns it on the lost-object case: returning a lost object is a Torah מצוה, so how does the זקן's dignity push it aside?

phrases.english: Why?
Let us say: "There is no wisdom and no understanding
and no counsel against ה׳"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the dignity case in the ברייתא from Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a זקן may ignore a lost object because of his dignity.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Human considerations should never override a Torah command, because there is no counsel against ה׳.

steps.title: The Torah itself made this exception
steps.stepSummary: The lost-object case is different because the Torah itself wrote 'וְהִתְעַלַּמְתָּ מֵהֶם', which shows that sometimes you may ignore it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because it is written: 'and you shall disregard them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the זקן is not going against ה׳. The Torah's own words allow him to look away in some cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody is overriding the Torah here. The פסוק itself builds in the exception, so following it is obeying ה׳, not working against Him.

phrases.english: It is different there,
since it is written: "and you shall disregard them."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a פסוק that makes a special exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the זקן was letting dignity beat a Torah law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah itself permits ignoring the object in this case, so there is no conflict with 'no counsel against ה׳'.

steps.title: Can we learn a general rule from this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the Torah lets dignity win in the lost-object case, why not learn from it that dignity beats every Torah law?
steps.simpleTranslation: So let us learn from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests using the lost-object case as a model for all Torah laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 showed one place where the Torah lets dignity win. The question is whether that one case can teach a general rule for every other מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn from it

phrases.english: And let us learn from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer of Step 18 and tries to stretch it into a general rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the lost-object case is only a special exception.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the Torah shows dignity winning in one place, we should apply that to all prohibitions.

steps.title: Money laws can't teach prohibition laws
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we do not learn rules about איסור (prohibitions) from rules about ממון (money).
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not learn prohibitions from money matters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks the attempt to make a general rule. A lost object is a money matter, and other laws are prohibitions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning a lost object is about someone's money. The Torah can be more flexible with money, so this case cannot prove that dignity overrides real איסורים. That means the search for a proof has to go on.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not learn (one from the other)

steps.whatToRemember: The lost-object case is a real Torah exception for dignity, but it is about money, so it cannot prove that dignity overrides איסורים.

phrases.english: Prohibition from money matters
we do not learn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the two kinds of law are different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lost-object case could teach that dignity beats all Torah laws.
steps.terutzMaskana: Money laws are different, so no general rule about prohibitions can come from them.

steps.title: New challenge: the נזיר and 'his sister'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא on 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ'. A person on his way to bring his קרבן פסח or do his son's ברית מילה must not become טמא for a relative who died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Why does the Torah say 'and for his sister'? Suppose someone was going to slaughter his פסח and to circumcise his son, and he heard that a relative of his died. Might he go back and become impure? You said: he shall not become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new proof with 'come and hear.' It is setting up a case where an important מצוה is up against a person's duty to a dead relative. The point it wants to make begins in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first rules that even the honor of burying your own relative does not let you skip the פסח or the מילה. This is the base the גמרא will build on to test whether dignity can override a Torah prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the פסוק need to say this?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't stop here thinking the proof is finished. This is only the opening of the ברייתא; the part that matters for dignity comes next.

phrases.english: Come and hear.
"And for his sister": why does the verse say it?
phrases.notes: במדבר 6:7, about a נזיר who may not become impure even for close relatives.

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה הוֹלֵךְ לִשְׁחוֹט אֶת פִּסְחוֹ,
phrases.english: Suppose one was going to slaughter his Paschal lamb,
and to circumcise his son,
and he heard that a relative of his died,
might he turn back and become impure?
You said: he shall not become impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the lost-object challenge was limited to money laws in Step 20, the גמרא opens a fresh challenge that deals with a real איסור.
steps.raayaObject: Whether dignity can override a Torah prohibition. The ברייתא continues in step 22 and finishes on the next amud.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' about a נזיר.

steps.title: The verse limits the ban to relatives, not a body with no one to bury it
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises the possibility that the person on his way to a מצוה may not become טמא even for a מת מצוה. It answers from the word 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' that the ban applies only to his sister, meaning relatives.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: just as he does not become טמא for his relatives, so too he does not become טמא for a מת מצוה. That is why the verse says 'and for his sister.' It is for his sister that he does not become טמא...
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going. It first suggests a wrong idea, that even a מת מצוה is off-limits, and then starts to show from the פסוק that this idea is wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'יָכוֹל' brings in a possible mistake: treating a מת מצוה just like a relative. The extra word 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' narrows the ban to relatives only, who have other people to bury them. This prepares the point the גמרא needs: burying a מת מצוה, which is a matter of human dignity, pushes aside even the מצוה he was on his way to do.

keyTerms.meaning: "I might have thought": opens a mistaken idea that the ברייתא will reject
Becomes ritually impure, here by dealing with a dead body
A dead body with no one else to bury it, so whoever finds it must bury it
"The verse teaches": brings the פסוק that settles the question

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying he may never become טמא. The ban covers only relatives. For a מת מצוה the ברייתא is about to say he must become טמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the part of the ברייתא the גמרא needs to prove that כבוד הבריות can push aside a Torah rule. Here, a מת מצוה pushes aside the rule against becoming טמא on the way to a מצוה.

phrases.english: I might have thought: just as he does not become impure for them
phrases.notes: "Them" means the relatives listed in the verse: father, mother, brother, sister.

phrases.english: so too he does not become impure for a מת מצוה
the verse teaches: "And for his sister"
it is for his sister that he does not become impure,

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא לָהֶם כָּךְ אֵינוֹ מִטַּמֵּא לְמֵת מִצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from Step 21, moving from the rule about relatives to the exception for a מת מצוה.
steps.raayaObject: That human dignity (כבוד הבריות) can push aside a Torah prohibition
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's reading of the word 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' (במדבר 6:7), which limits the ban on becoming טמא to relatives and so makes room for a מת מצוה
